\chapter{Good Afternoon}
\label{ch:la-good-afternoon}
\hlchaptermodality{36}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Latin in the afternoon with salvē or salvēte, and explain why nothing more is needed.}

One Roman day in four meetings — morning, afternoon, evening, and parting at night — with salvē and valē marked as the attested pair and the three bonus phrases marked as modern.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[salvē (post merīdiem)]{salvē (post merīdiem) — the one that isn't there}

\label{lesson:LA-C36-salve-post-meridiem}



\begin{quote}
Three lessons in a row, you've met a modern phrase built on real (if sometimes invisible) Latin grammar for \textquotedblleft{}good \_\_\_.\textquotedblright{} This lesson is different: there's honestly nothing to build.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Bonam noctem}, \textbf{bonum māne}, and \textbf{bonum vesperum} are all modern, pedagogical phrases — not classically attested — but each pairs \emph{bonus} directly with a \textbf{single noun} in the accusative: \emph{noctem}, \emph{māne}, \emph{vesperum}. \textquotedblleft{}Good afternoon\textquotedblright{} can't take that same shape, because you already learned last lesson that Latin has \textbf{no simplex noun} for \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} at all — there's no \emph{afternoonem} for \emph{bonus} to modify. \textbf{Bonum post merīdiem} doesn't work: \emph{post merīdiem} (\textquotedblleft{}after noon\textquotedblright{}) is a whole \textbf{prepositional phrase}, not a noun, so \emph{bonus} has nothing to agree with. A three-word workaround, \textbf{bonum tempus pōmerīdiānum} (\textquotedblleft{}good afternoon time\textquotedblright{}), actually \textbf{is} grammatical — \emph{pōmerīdiānus} (\textquotedblleft{}of the afternoon\textquotedblright{}) is a real word Cicero himself uses, and here \emph{bonus} agrees with a genuine noun, \emph{tempus} (\textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}). But it's a \textbf{periphrasis}, not a direct two-word match for the other three phrases — and it isn't itself attested anywhere as something Romans actually said as a greeting.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item why \textquotedblleft{}bonum post merīdiem\textquotedblright{} doesn't work — no noun for bonus to agree with; why \textquotedblleft{}bonum tempus pōmerīdiānum\textquotedblright{} DOES work, but isn't attested as a real greeting
  \item the grammatical adjective — pōmerīdiānum, \textquotedblleft{}of the afternoon\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Latin have a two-word phrase for \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon\textquotedblright{} the way it has \emph{bonum vesperum} for evening? (\textbf{No} — Latin has no simplex noun for \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} for \emph{bonus} to pair with.) Is there ANY grammatical Latin phrase at all? (\textbf{Yes} — \emph{bonum tempus pōmerīdiānum} is real grammar, but a three-word periphrasis, not attested as an actual greeting.) What did Romans say in the afternoon instead? (\textbf{Salvē} — the same everyday greeting from Chapter 1.) Why doesn't \emph{bonum post merīdiem} work grammatically? (\emph{Post merīdiem} is a whole prepositional phrase, not a single noun \emph{bonus} can agree with.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[salvē / salvēte]{salvē — the greeting that does not watch the clock}

\label{lesson:LA-C36-timeless-salve}



\begin{quote}
Latin cannot build a neat two-word \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon.\textquotedblright{} What did Romans actually need in that time slot? Nothing beyond a greeting you already know.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Salvē} to one person and \textbf{salvēte} to several people mean \textquotedblleft{}be well.\textquotedblright{} Neither form contains a morning, afternoon, or evening boundary. Romans could use the greeting whenever they met someone.

English encourages a learner to search for four matched clock-based formulas. Latin everyday greetings do not divide the day that way. The missing afternoon formula is therefore not a hole in Roman conversation.

The time-of-day arc now has three different kinds of evidence:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a real institution, the morning \textbf{salūtātiō}
  \item grammatical but modern phrases such as \textbf{bonam noctem}
  \item no dedicated formula at all for afternoon—just \textbf{salvē}
\end{itemize}

Learning those differences is more faithful than forcing four symmetrical translations into Latin.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}salvē\textquotedblright{} — be well, to one person
  \item \textquotedblleft{}salvēte\textquotedblright{} — be well, to several people
  \item the time restriction — none
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What can one Roman say on meeting another in the afternoon? (\textbf{Salvē.}) What is the plural? (\textbf{Salvēte.}) Do these words encode a time of day? (\textbf{No.}) Why is there no conversational gap? (\textbf{The everyday greeting already works whenever people meet.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — one whole day, in the words you have}

\label{lesson:LA-C36-practice}



\begin{quote}
Nine chapters of time-of-day words end here. This is the one place they all have to work at once — four meetings, one day, and no inventing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — morning to night, with the honest label on each line}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Morning.} A: \textbf{Salvē! Quid agis?}  B: \textbf{Valeō. Salvē!}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Afternoon.} A: \textbf{Salvē!}  B: \textbf{Salvē!}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Evening.} A: \textbf{Bonum vesperum!}  B: \textbf{Salvē!}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Parting at night.} A: \textbf{Bonam noctem!}  B: \textbf{Valē!}
\end{quote}

Now the label, which is half the payoff. \textbf{Salvē}, \textbf{salvēte} and \textbf{valē} are genuinely Roman and carry no clock inside them, so they work in every one of those four rows. The three \emph{bonus} phrases — \emph{bonum māne}, \emph{bonum vesperum}, \emph{bonam noctem} — are well-formed modern teaching phrases, not lines from any surviving Roman text. And the afternoon row has only \emph{salvē} in it, because Latin never had a noun for \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} for \emph{bonus} to agree with.

So the safe rule you leave with: \textbf{when in doubt, salvē on arrival and valē on departure, at any hour.}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Run through:} all four rows aloud, both voices
  \item \emph{Choose:} mid-afternoon, and you want to be Roman $\to$ \textbf{salvē}
  \item \emph{Say it:} why it is \emph{noctem} and \emph{vesperum}, not \emph{nox} and \emph{vesper} — Latin wishes take the accusative
  \item \emph{Choose:} a room full of people $\to$ \textbf{salvēte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two words in the whole day-cycle are genuinely attested? (\textbf{Salvē} and \textbf{valē}.) What did Rome actually have in the morning instead of a phrase? (The \textbf{salūtātiō} — a dawn visit, an action.) Why can \emph{bonum māne} not show the accusative rule? (\emph{Māne} is \textbf{neuter}; neuters never distinguish the two cases.)
\end{tcolorbox}
